lead: Sampling converts a continuous-time signal into a sequence of numbers, and this unit follows that sequence from the first sample to the output of a discrete-time system. After it you can state and apply the sampling theorem, spot and prevent aliasing, handle band-pass and sample-and-hold sampling, size a quantizer, and solve discrete-time LTI systems by the convolution sum and by difference equations.
about: The unit follows a signal from the analog world into the discrete world. The first chapter states the sampling theorem and shows how an ideal low-pass filter rebuilds the signal; the second explains what goes wrong below the Nyquist rate and why an analog filter sits before the sampler. The third covers band-pass sampling and the aperture effect of practical, flat-top sampling, and the fourth, which only a few syllabi list, rounds the held samples to a finite set of levels. The last two chapters move to discrete-time LTI systems: the convolution sum, and linear constant-coefficient difference equations with their recursive solution and pole-based stability. The discrete-time Fourier transform and the Z-transform are pointed to here and taught under Z-transform and discrete Fourier analysis.

chapters.idea: A signal whose highest frequency is f_max is fully described by its samples taken faster than 2 f_max, and an ideal low-pass filter rebuilds it.
chapters.depth: State the theorem for a band-limited signal: exact reconstruction needs f_s > 2 f_max, where f_s is the sampling rate in Hz. Define the Nyquist rate 2 f_max, the Nyquist frequency f_s/2, and the sampling interval T_s = 1/f_s seconds. Build the impulse-train model x_s(t) = x(t)·Σ δ(t − nT_s) and sketch the sampled spectrum: copies of X(f) centred at multiples of f_s, each scaled by 1/T_s. Give ideal reconstruction as a low-pass filter of cutoff f_s/2 and gain T_s, and the interpolation formula x(t) = Σ x(nT_s) sinc((t − nT_s)/T_s). Some syllabi call this the Nyquist–Shannon or Whittaker–Shannon theorem, and call reconstruction ideal interpolation. Keep the derivation at spectrum-sketch level.

figure.title: Sampling and ideal reconstruction
figure.aria: A band-limited signal with highest frequency 450 Hz enters a sampler clocked at 1 kHz, giving samples 1 ms apart, and an ideal low-pass filter with 500 Hz cutoff rebuilds the signal.

chapters.example: x(t) = 3 cos(2π·200t) + 2 cos(2π·450t) volts is sampled at f_s = 1000 Hz. Find f_max, the Nyquist rate, T_s and the reconstruction filter cutoff, and check for overlap of the spectral copies. Answer: f_max = 450 Hz, Nyquist rate = 900 Hz, and 1000 Hz > 900 Hz so sampling is safe. T_s = 1 ms and the reconstruction filter cutoff is f_s/2 = 500 Hz. Copies sit at 0, ±1000, ±2000 Hz; the highest baseband component is 450 Hz and the lowest upper copy is 1000 − 450 = 550 Hz, so a 100 Hz guard band separates them.
chapters.trap: Swapping the Nyquist rate (2 f_max) with the Nyquist frequency (f_s/2), and dropping the 1/T_s gain of the reconstruction filter. Also, sampling exactly at f_s = 2 f_max is not enough for a sinusoid sitting at f_max: its amplitude and phase cannot be recovered.
chapters.prereq: Unit 3 for the Fourier transform, the sinc spectrum and ideal filters; Unit 1 for standard signals.
chapters.leave: The folding rule and anti-aliasing filters to 5.2, the band-pass case to 5.3, quantization to 5.4.

chapters.idea: Sampling below 2 f_max makes high frequencies reappear at low frequencies, and only a filter placed before the sampler can stop it.
chapters.depth: Derive aliasing as spectral overlap when f_s < 2 f_max. Give the folding rule: a component at f comes out at the frequency nearest to zero among |f − k f_s| for integer k, and show with a small table of folded values. Show that cos(2π f t) and cos(2π (f_s − f) t) give identical samples, so the two are indistinguishable after sampling. Define the anti-aliasing filter: an analog low-pass filter before the sampler with cutoff at or below f_s/2; its order follows from the required stop-band attenuation and the width of the transition band. State clearly that no digital step after sampling can remove an alias. Some syllabi use the names fold-over and anti-aliasing prefilter.

figure.aria: A 700 Hz cosine and a 300 Hz cosine cross at every integer sample index, so the two signals give exactly the same samples when the rate is 1000 Hz.

chapters.example: A speech signal occupying 300 Hz to 3400 Hz is sampled at 8000 Hz; show that it does not alias. Then a tone cos(2π·700t) volts is sampled at 1000 Hz; find the frequency of the reconstructed tone. Answer: 3400 Hz < 4000 Hz = f_s/2, so the speech is safe with a 600 Hz guard band. For the tone, f_s/2 = 500 Hz < 700 Hz, so it folds to |700 − 1000| = 300 Hz and the output is cos(2π·300t) volts, same amplitude. A tone at 1300 Hz would give the same samples.
chapters.trap: Believing a faster sampler cures aliasing already caused by an out-of-band interferer, or placing the anti-aliasing filter after the sampler. The cutoff must be at most f_s/2, not 2 f_max.
chapters.prereq: 5.1 for the sampling theorem and the spectrum copies; Unit 3 for the ideal low-pass response.
chapters.leave: The band-pass version of the theorem to 5.3; digital filters to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: A signal with a narrow band far from zero can be sampled below its top frequency, and a real sample-and-hold circuit quietly attenuates high frequencies.
chapters.depth: Compare the two theorems. Low-pass: f_s > 2 f_max. Band-pass: a signal occupying f_L to f_H, bandwidth B = f_H − f_L, can be sampled below 2 f_H; usable rates are f_s = 2 f_H/m with m an integer not exceeding floor(f_H/B), provided the shifted band lands inside 0 to f_s/2 without overlap. Show the placement check with the two inequalities f_H ≤ m f_s/2 and f_L ≥ (m − 1) f_s/2. Then practical sampling: the sample is held for τ seconds, giving the aperture response H(f) = τ sinc(f τ), which droops and has its first zero at 1/τ. For a full-period hold τ = T_s the gain at f_s/2 is 2/π ≈ 0.637, about −3.9 dB, and it is corrected by an inverse-sinc filter. Mention practical interpolation by a zero-order hold followed by a smoothing filter.

figure.aria: The aperture response starts at 1, falls to about 0.64 at 2 kHz and reaches zero at 4 kHz, while the ideal response stays flat at 1.

chapters.example: A signal has components only between 5 kHz and 6 kHz. Find a valid band-pass sampling rate well below the low-pass requirement of 12 kHz, and check that the copies do not overlap. Answer: B = 1 kHz, f_H = 6 kHz, so m = floor(6/1) = 6 and f_s = 2 f_H/m = 2 kHz. Check f_H ≤ m f_s/2 = 6 kHz (true, equal) and f_L ≥ (m − 1) f_s/2 = 5 kHz (true, equal). The band lands in 0 to 1 kHz with no overlap, and a band-pass filter with a 2 kHz sampling clock recovers it.
chapters.trap: Applying f_s > 2 f_max to a band-pass signal and insisting on 12 kHz, or picking f_s = 2B without checking the placement inequalities. Also forgetting that aperture droop needs correction at the band edge.
chapters.prereq: 5.1 and 5.2 for the low-pass theorem and the folding picture; Unit 3 for sinc spectra and band-pass filters.
chapters.leave: Quantization of the held samples to 5.4; the Z-domain treatment of the hold circuit to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: A sample of finite word length must be rounded to one of 2^n levels, and that rounding is modelled as added noise.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this topic. Uniform quantization: with L = 2^n levels for an n-bit quantizer over a range x_min to x_max, the step size is Δ = (x_max − x_min)/L. A mid-rise quantizer puts levels at odd multiples of Δ/2 and the error is bounded by ±Δ/2. Treat the error as uniform random noise of power Δ²/12, giving the signal-to-quantization-noise ratio 6.02n + 1.76 dB for a full-scale sinusoid. Define resolution, overload (clipping) error, and mention companding with μ-law and A-law and the noise reduction from oversampling. Keep it to one page: the exam wants Δ, error bound and the SQNR formula.

figure.aria: A staircase with 1 V steps jumping between levels 0.5 V, 1.5 V and so on, while the ideal quantizer output is a straight line through the origin.

chapters.example: A 3-bit uniform quantizer covers 0 V to 8 V. Find Δ, the maximum quantization error, the output for an input sample of 3.4 V with a mid-rise quantizer, and the SQNR for a full-scale sinusoid. Answer: L = 2³ = 8 levels, so Δ = 8/8 = 1 V and the maximum error is Δ/2 = 0.5 V. Levels sit at 0.5, 1.5, ..., 7.5 V, so 3.4 V becomes 3.5 V with error 0.1 V. SQNR = 6.02(3) + 1.76 = 19.8 dB, which also follows from 10 log₁₀(8 ÷ (1/12)) with a full-scale sine of amplitude 4 V.
chapters.trap: Using Δ instead of Δ/2 as the maximum error, writing the number of levels as 2^n − 1, and applying the 6.02n + 1.76 dB formula to a signal that is not full-scale sinusoidal.
chapters.prereq: 5.1 to 5.3 for where the samples come from; Unit 1 for signal power and average value.
chapters.leave: Coding and source compression to a communications course; digital filter design to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: A discrete-time LTI system is completely described by its impulse response, and its output is the convolution sum of input and impulse response.
chapters.depth: Discrete-time signals as sequences x[n] with integer n, including periodicity with period N. Define the unit impulse δ[n] and unit step u[n], and the impulse response h[n] as the response to δ[n]. Linearity plus time invariance gives y[n] = Σ_k x[k] h[n − k] = Σ_k h[k] x[n − k], the convolution sum. Show two evaluation methods: sliding the flipped h[n] along x[n], and the table of products. List the properties: commutative, associative, distributive, identity element δ[n], and the length rule for finite sequences (N₁ + N₂ − 1). Causality means h[n] = 0 for n < 0; BIBO stability means Σ |h[n]| is finite. Define the frequency response H(e^{jω}) = Σ h[n] e^{−jωn} and the step response, without deriving transforms.

figure.title: Convolution of x[n] and h[n]
figure.aria: Three rows of numbers: x[n] = 2, 1, 3 convolved with h[n] = 1, 2 gives y[n] = 2, 5, 5, 6, with y[1] = 2·2 + 1·1 = 5 marked.

chapters.example: x[n] = [2, 1, 3] for n = 0, 1, 2 and h[n] = [1, 2] for n = 0, 1. Find y[n] by the convolution sum. Answer: y[0] = 2·1 = 2; y[1] = 2·2 + 1·1 = 5; y[2] = 1·2 + 3·1 = 5; y[3] = 3·2 = 6, so y[n] = [2, 5, 5, 6], of length 3 + 2 − 1 = 4. Second part: is the system with h[n] = (0.5)^n u[n] BIBO stable? Σ |h[n]| = 1/(1 − 0.5) = 2, finite, so yes.
chapters.trap: Not flipping h[n] in the sliding method, and losing the leading or trailing sample so the output length is wrong. For stability, testing only the first few terms of h[n] instead of the whole sum.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for discrete-time standard signals and system properties; Unit 2 for the convolution integral, which this mirrors.
chapters.leave: DTFT, DFT and Z-transform methods to Unit 6; difference-equation solving to 5.6.

chapters.idea: A recursive difference equation gives the output sample by sample from past outputs and inputs, and its poles decide stability.
chapters.depth: Write the general linear constant-coefficient difference equation y[n] = −Σ_{k=1}^{N} a_k y[n − k] + Σ_{m=0}^{M} b_m x[n − m], and define its order, the recursive (IIR) and non-recursive (FIR) cases. Solve by iteration from the initial conditions y[−1], y[−2], and then in closed form as natural response plus forced response, with natural modes λ^n from the roots of the characteristic equation. Draw the block diagram of adders, unit delays z⁻¹ and multipliers. For causal systems, all poles inside the unit circle means stable, on the circle means marginally stable, outside means unstable. State that the Z-transform in Unit 6 finds the same response faster, and that here the work stays in the time domain.

figure.title: First-order recursive system
figure.aria: Block diagram of y[n] = x[n] + 0.5 y[n−1]: the output goes through a unit delay and a 0.5 multiplier and returns to the adder.

chapters.example: Solve y[n] − 0.5 y[n − 1] = x[n] with x[n] = u[n] and y[n] = 0 for n < 0. Iterate for n = 0 to 3, then find the closed form and check stability. Answer: y[0] = 1; y[1] = 0.5(1) + 1 = 1.5; y[2] = 0.5(1.5) + 1 = 1.75; y[3] = 1.875. The forced response is the constant 2, since 2 − 0.5(2) = 1, and the natural response is −(0.5)^n chosen to make y[0] = 1, so y[n] = 2 − (0.5)^n for n ≥ 0. The single pole is at z = 0.5, inside the unit circle, so the system is stable.
chapters.trap: Getting the signs of the a_k wrong when rewriting the equation in recursive form, and taking y[0] instead of y[−1] as the initial condition, which shifts the whole solution.
chapters.prereq: 5.5 for convolution and impulse response; Unit 1 for unit step and unit impulse; basic algebra of complex roots.
chapters.leave: Z-transform solution, region of convergence and pole-zero plots to Unit 6.
